claims: Yellow fever, typhoid, and Japanese encephalitis are not common in the United States.
The CDC recommends consulting a healthcare provider or travel clinic 4–6 weeks before departure to allow time for vaccines to take effect and for multi-dose series to be completed.
Routine vaccines include measles-mumps-rubella (MMR), diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, varicella (chickenpox), polio, and yearly flu shot.
Hepatitis A vaccine is recommended for travelers to most countries, particularly those with uncertain water or food safety.
Typhoid vaccine is recommended for travelers going to parts of Asia, Africa, and South America, especially if visiting smaller cities, villages, or rural areas.
Yellow fever vaccine is required for entry into certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South America.
Proof of vaccination (the "Yellow Card") is required for yellow fever.
The "Yellow Card" becomes valid 10 days after administration.
Meningococcal vaccine is required for travelers to Saudi Arabia for Hajj or Umrah pilgrimages.
Meningococcal vaccine is recommended for the "meningitis belt" of Africa.
As of March 2026, the CDC has issued alerts for increased polio risk in over 30 countries.
